identity.title: On the Role of Computation in Reinforcement Learning

problem.claim: The paper asks how available computation affects RL policy learning and whether fixed-parameter policies can benefit from additional computation.

gap.claim: The standard RL framework lacks a formal language for these questions, while static neural-network architectures conflate computation with parameter count.

contributions.claim: Formalizes compute-bounded policies and proves that higher-compute policies can solve problems and generalize to longer-horizon tasks beyond lower-compute policies' scope.
Proposes a minimal architecture capable of using a variable amount of computation, building on algorithmic learning and model-free planning.
Reports experiments across 31 online and offline RL tasks evaluating compute scaling and longer-horizon generalization.

stated_novelty.claim: The stated new distinction is to formalize compute-bounded policies and introduce a minimal variable-compute architecture for RL.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that the proposed architecture achieves stronger performance when using more computation across 31 tasks.
The authors report stronger generalization on longer-horizon test tasks than standard feedforward and deep residual networks using up to five times more parameters.
The authors report theoretical results that higher-compute policies can solve and generalize to longer-horizon tasks outside the scope of lower-compute policies.

narrative_sequence.summary: Asks how computation affects RL learning and whether fixed-parameter policies benefit from additional computation.
Identifies the lack of a formal language and the confounding of compute with parameter count in static neural architectures.
Formalizes compute-bounded policies and states higher-compute advantages for problem solving and longer-horizon generalization.
Introduces a minimal architecture with variable compute, drawing on algorithmic learning and model-free planning.

The authors report complementary experiments on 31 tasks spanning online and offline RL: stronger performance with more compute and stronger generalization on longer-horizon test tasks compared with standard feedforward networks or deep residual networks using up to five times more parameters.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates computation from parameter count by formalizing compute-bounded policies and comparing variable-compute policies with networks using up to five times more parameters.

lessons.interpretation: This framing makes computational scaling an explicit experimental variable rather than a proxy for model size.
lessons.application: When studying scaling, define a compute budget independently and include comparisons that vary parameters without equating them to computation.
lessons.exception: This move may be unsuitable when the target deployment fixes architecture and inference cost jointly.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the formal compute model, policy assumptions, task domains, or proof conditions.
It does not report quantitative performance, uncertainty, statistical procedures, or exact compute budgets.
The phrase “up to 5 times more parameters” does not establish equality of training or inference compute.

editorial_revisions.before: Reports complementary experiments on 31 online and offline RL tasks, including comparisons with parameter-matched alternatives.
editorial_revisions.after: The authors report complementary experiments on 31 tasks spanning online and offline RL: stronger performance with more compute and stronger generalization on longer-horizon test tasks compared with standard feedforward networks or deep residual networks using up to five times more parameters.
